\chapter{Weather}
\label{ch:ar-weather}
\hlchaptermodality{18}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what the weather is doing in Arabic -- hot, cold, or raining.}

Say aṭ-ṭaqs, then the verbless al-jaw ḥārr / al-jaw bārid, then innahā tumṭir, which does take a verb.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{الطقس} (aṭ-ṭaqs)}{الطقس (aṭ-ṭaqs)}]{\ar{الطقس} — weather and ritual, one root}

\label{lesson:AR-C18-al-taqs}



\begin{quote}
Here's an unexpected pairing: Arabic's word for \textquotedblleft{}weather\textquotedblright{} shares its root with the word for religious \textquotedblleft{}rites.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \ar{طقس} — weather, and its plural means \textquotedblleft{}rites\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{\ar{الطقس}} (\emph{aṭ-ṭaqs}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the weather}\textquotedblright{} — from root \textbf{\ar{ط}-\ar{ق}-\ar{س}} (\emph{ṭ-q-s}). Its plural, \textbf{\ar{طقوس}} (\emph{ṭuqūs}), means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{rites, religious ceremonies, liturgy}\textquotedblright{} — the same root covering both \textquotedblleft{}atmospheric conditions\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}prescribed ritual observances.\textquotedblright{} (Casual speech often prefers \textbf{\ar{الجو}} (\emph{al-jaw}, \textquotedblleft{}the atmosphere\textquotedblright{}) instead, keeping \emph{aṭ-ṭaqs} for more formal or written use.)

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \ar{الجو} \ar{حار} / \emph{bārid} — hot and cold, still verbless}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{الجو} \ar{حار}.} — \textquotedblleft{}It's hot.\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the atmosphere {[}is{]} hot}.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{al-jaw ḥārr.}) \emph{al-jaw bārid.} — \textquotedblleft{}It's cold.\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the atmosphere {[}is{]} cold}.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Same pattern as \textbf{\ar{كم} \ar{عمرك؟}} from the AGE lesson: \textbf{no verb \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{}} at all — just two nouns/adjectives sitting side by side.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \emph{innahā tumṭir} — but rain gets its OWN personal verb}
\begin{quote}
\emph{innahā tumṭir.} — \textquotedblleft{}It's raining.\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{she is raining}.\textquotedblright{} (From \textbf{\ar{مطر}}, \emph{maṭar}, \textquotedblleft{}rain\textquotedblright{}; the same root gives \emph{tumṭir}, \textquotedblleft{}is raining.\textquotedblright{})
\end{quote}

Unlike \emph{hot} and \emph{cold}, rain isn't a verbless adjective sentence — Arabic uses an actual \textbf{personal verb}, \emph{tumṭir} (\textquotedblleft{}is raining\textquotedblright{}), with a \textbf{feminine dummy pronoun}, \emph{innahā} (\textquotedblleft{}she/it\textquotedblright{}), standing in as the subject. So within Arabic's own weather vocabulary, hot/cold stay verbless while rain gets a real, conjugated verb — echoing the same \textquotedblleft{}rain behaves differently from other weather\textquotedblright{} pattern Latin shows in its dedicated \emph{pluit}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}aṭ-ṭaqs\textquotedblright{} — weather, same root as \textquotedblleft{}ṭuqūs,\textquotedblright{} rites
  \item \textquotedblleft{}al-jaw ḥārr. al-jaw bārid.\textquotedblright{} — it's hot/cold, no verb
  \item \textquotedblleft{}innahā tumṭir\textquotedblright{} — it's raining, with an actual verb
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the plural of \textbf{\ar{طقس}} mean, and what's the connection to \textquotedblleft{}weather\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\ar{طقوس}}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{rites, religious ceremonies}\textquotedblright{} — sharing the same root.) Do \textbf{\ar{الجو} \ar{حار}} and \emph{al-jaw bārid} use a verb? (\textbf{No} — verbless, like \emph{kam ʿumruka?}.) Does \emph{innahā tumṭir} use a verb? (\textbf{Yes} — \emph{tumṭir}, \textquotedblleft{}is raining,\textquotedblright{} with a feminine dummy pronoun.)
\end{tcolorbox}
